宗像大社 | image = Honden of Munakata Grand Shrine (Hetsu Shrine).JPG | caption = Hetsu-no-Miya Honden of 1578 ([[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ICP]]) | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|53|N|130|30|50|E|display=inline,title|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1100}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = Munakata Shrine | deity = {{ubl|Ichikishima Hime-no-Kami|Tagitsu Hime-no-Kami|Tagori Hime-no-Kami}} | founded_by = | established = | date_destroyed = | location = 2331, Tashima, [[Munakata, Fukuoka|Munakata]]
[[Fukuoka Prefecture|Fukuoka]] [[〒]]811-3505
1811, [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]], Munakata
Fukuoka 〒811-3701 | website = {{URL|http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Munakata Taisha'''|宗像大社}} is a collection of three [[Shinto]] [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] located in [[Munakata, Fukuoka|Munakata]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the head of the approximately 6,000 Munakata shrines all over the country. Although the name Munakata Taisha refers to all three shrines—Hetsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū—it is commonly used to refer to Hetsu-gū alone. As documented in Japan's second oldest book, ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', the shrines are devoted to the {{Nihongo|three Munakata goddesses|宗像三女神|Munakata-sanjojin}}. These ''[[kami]]'' are believed to be daughters of the goddess [[Amaterasu]], the ancestress of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial family]] or to be the daughters of [[Susanoo]], who has also been worshipped there for many years as the god of mariners, and he has come to be worshipped as the god of traffic safety on land as well. Munakata Taisha is also home to many Japanese treasures. Hetsu-gū's ''[[honden]]'' (main shrine) and ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' (main prayer hall) are both designated [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Properties]] and the precincts are a [[Monuments of Japan|Historic Site]].{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/2661 |title=宗像神社境内 |trans-title=Munakata Jinja Precinct |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=15 June 2012}} The {{Nihongo|Shinpō-kan|神寶館}}, the shrine's treasure hall located on the east corner of Hetsu-gū's grounds, houses many important relics including six [[National Treasures of Japan]]. Over 120,000 artifacts housed in the Shinpō-kan were unearthed on [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]].{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |title=Stroll through Munakata History |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081013024006/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |archive-date=2008-10-13}} It was formerly an imperial shrine of the first rank (官幣大社, ''kanpei taisha'') in the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft}} refers collectively to the three shrines: '''Okitsu Shrine''' (沖津宮) on [[Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|Okinoshima]], '''Nakatsu Shrine''' (中津宮) on {{ill|Ōshima (Fukuoka)|ja|筑前大島|Ōshima (Fukuoka)=Ōshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Chikuzen Ōshima|12=draft}}, and the main shrine, '''Hetsu Shrine''' (辺津宮) in {{ill|Munakata, Fukuoka|ja|宗像市|12=draft}} Tajima. However, in modern usage, "Munakata Taisha" often refers only to Hetsu Shrine. Locally, Hetsu Shrine is known as "Tajima-sama" (田島さま). Nakatsu Shrine has a remote {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship site|12=draft}} for Okitsu Shrine called '''Etsu Shrine''' (瀛津宮) on Chikuzen Ōshima. Geographically, Nakatsu Shrine is 11 km from Hetsu Shrine, and Okitsu Shrine is another 49 km away, all aligned in a straight line. As one of the oldest shrines in Japan, Munakata Taisha is mentioned in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, and has been historically significant due to its location along the sea routes connecting Japan to the continent and the Korean Peninsula. Traditionally revered as a protector of maritime and travel safety, it continues to be widely worshiped today as the guardian deity of all roads, under the name {{ill|Three_Munakata_Goddesses|lt=Dōshunomikoto|ja|道主貴|12=draft}}. Consequently, in Fukuoka Prefecture and surrounding areas, it is common to see cars displaying Munakata Taisha {{ill|stickers|ja|シール|12=draft}}, and many people visit the shrine's prayer hall to have their new vehicles blessed. Additionally, the concept of a vehicle-mounted traffic safety {{ill|Omamori|ja|お守り|12=draft}} is said to have originated at Munakata Taisha. {{ill|Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Okinoshima|ja|沖ノ島|12=draft}}, where Okitsu Shrine is located, has long been a key maritime transit point. Since ancient times, it has been considered forbidden to disclose anything seen or heard on the island, leading to its moniker "Ofugen-sama" (お不言さま, "The Island of Silence"). The entire island is regarded as a sacred body, and to this day, women are prohibited from setting foot on it, while men must undergo a {{ill|Misogi|ja|禊|12=draft}} purification ritual before landing. Some criticize this as gender discrimination, but a traditional belief states that the island's deity, {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|田心姫神|12=draft}}, is a female kami who would grow jealous and curse any woman who set foot there. However, the accuracy of this explanation is uncertain. Archaeological excavations of Okinoshima, conducted over more than a decade since 1954, uncovered numerous ancient ritual sites and offerings dating from the 4th to 9th centuries, including decorated artifacts, as well as stone tools and pottery from the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代|12=draft}} and {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}}. Due to this wealth of artifacts, the island is often referred to as the "Marine {{ill|Shōsōin|ja|正倉院|12=draft}}." These discoveries suggest that Okinoshima has been a religious center for maritime people since prehistoric times. Today, the island is designated as a safe harbor for emergency shelter during typhoons. A {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft}} plaque displayed in the main shrine hall was personally inscribed by {{ill|Prince Fushimi Sadanaru|ja|伏見宮貞愛親王|12=draft}}, while the "Munakata Shrine" plaque was written by imperial envoy {{ill|Hamaguchi Akitaka|ja|葉室顕孝|12=draft}}, a {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft}} Gon Dainagon. In 2009, an initiative led by [[:ja:Sakuji Yoshimura|Sakuji Yoshimura]], an [[Egyptologist]], proposed designating Okinoshima and related Munakata heritage sites as a {{ill|lt=UNESCO World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site|ja|世界遺産|12=draft}}. That year, "Okitsu Shrine, Nakatsu Shrine, and Hetsu Shrine," along with "Okitsu Shrine {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=Worship Site|12=draft}} and all of Okinoshima," were added to Japan's tentative list under the title "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region." In 2015, it was officially nominated, and on July 2017, during the {{ill|UNESCO World Heritage Committee|ja|ユネスコ世界遺産委員会|12=draft}} session in {{ill|Kraków|ja|クラクフ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Poland|ja|ポーランド|12=draft}}, the site was officially inscribed as a World Heritage Site. ==Three shrines== [[File:Shimmon Gate of Munakata Grand Shrine (Hetsu Shrine) 2.JPG|thumb|250px|Gate of Hetsu-no-miya]] All three shrines are located in Fukuoka Prefecture, yet they are all on separate islands. The main shrine, Hetsu-gū, is located on the mainland of [[Kyūshū]]. Nakatsu-gū is established at the foot of Mt. Mitake on the island of [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] off the west coast of Kyūshū.{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ejx2.html |title=Munakata-taisha Nakatsu-gu Shrine |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=[[Japan National Tourist Organization]]}} The final shrine, Okitsu-gū, is on the island of [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] located in the middle of the [[Genkai Sea]]. The shrine occupies the entire island, therefore women are not allowed to set foot on the island and men must perform a [[misogi|purification ceremony]] before landing.{{cite web |url=http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |access-date=2008-06-02 |title=Muna Kata Tai Sha |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060125084824/http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |archive-date=2006-01-25}} In 2009 the three shrines were submitted for future inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage List]] as part of the serial nomination [[Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region]].{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5400/ |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=15 June 2012}}{{cite web |url=http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=World Heritage Promotion Committee of "Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region" |access-date=15 June 2012 |archive-date=5 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105154558/http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |title=Overview of Munakata City |access-date=2008-06-03 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829224830/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |archive-date=2010-08-29}} In July, 2017 Japan's Okinoshima Island gained UNESCO World Heritage Status.{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-40549909 |title=Japan's Okinoshima island gains Unesco World Heritage status |date=2017-07-09 |work=BBC News |access-date=2017-07-09 |language=en-GB}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! Shrine Name ! Enshrined deity ! Island location ! Coordinates |- | {{Nihongo|'''Hetsu-gū'''|辺津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ichikishimahime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|12=draft}}|市杵島姫神}} | [[Kyūshū]] | {{coord|33|49|53|N|130|30|50|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1100}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Nakatsu-gū'''|中津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|12=draft}}|湍津姫神}} | [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] | {{coord|33|53|49|N|130|25|56|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Okitsu-gū'''|沖津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|12=draft}}|田心姫神}} | [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] | {{coord|34|14|33|N|130|6|14|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |} [[File:Children born from the Challenge of Amaterasu and Susanoo-en.svg|thumb|240x240px|The three shrines correspond to the three daughters of Susanoo shown on the left]] == History == According to {{ill|tradition|ja|伝承|12=draft}}, the origins of {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft}} trace back to {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話|12=draft}}. During the {{ill|Oath of Amaterasu and Susanoo|ja|アマテラスとスサノオの誓約|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|12=draft}} shattered {{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft}}’s sword with her teeth and blew out fragments, from which the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|12=draft}} were born. The goddesses, carrying Amaterasu’s {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft}}, descended to the islands of Munakata floating in the Genkai Sea along the northern sea route to protect and aid her grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ja|ニニギノミコト|12=draft}}, establishing the origins of Munakata Taisha. In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, the only deities described as descending from the heavens before Ninigi-no-Mikoto’s {{ill|descent of the heavenly grandchild|ja|天孫降臨|12=draft}} are the Three Munakata Goddesses. This makes their recorded descent and enshrinement one of the earliest explicitly documented in the chronicles. Regarding the sacred objects representing the Three Munakata Goddesses, the {{ill|Chikuzen Province|ja|筑前国|12=draft}} {{ill|Fudoki|ja|風土記|12=draft}} states in its surviving fragments: {{quote|“According to the Saikaidō Fudoki, when the Munakata Great Deity descended from the heavens to settle at Sakimotoyama, a blue gem was placed at Okitsu Shrine, an eight-span purple gem at Nakatsu Shrine, and an eight-span mirror at Hetsu Shrine. These three objects became the forms of the deities and were enshrined in the three shrines. This tradition was later obscured, and the area was renamed ‘Munakata.’ The descendants of the deity, the Munakata clan, are the present-day Munakata Ason.”}} In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}}, the name "Munakata" is written as "Mune-Kata" (胸形), and also appears as "Munakata" (宗形) or "Mune-Kata" (胸肩). Some theories suggest that it originally referred to a water lagoon. Munakata Taisha was revered as the clan deity of the local people. It is said that when {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后|12=draft}} prayed for safe passage during her {{ill|conquest of the Three Han|ja|三韓征伐|12=draft}}, she experienced divine miracles, leading to the tradition of dispatching envoys to Munakata for rituals on significant occasions. Due to its importance, the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=draft}} honored the shrine, and each time the imperial capital was relocated, its deity was enshrined in the {{ill|Kashiko-dokoro|ja|賢所|12=draft}}, the imperial sanctuary. This highlights the deity’s reputation as a protector of maritime safety. With the introduction of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, Munakata was designated as a {{ill|shrine territory|ja|寺社領|12=draft}}, and the {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|1=Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|12=draft}}, a local ruling family, served as high priests while also governing the {{ill|shrine district|ja|神郡|12=draft}}. According to an inscription on a stone monument recording the lineage of the Munakata clan, two generations of their chieftains married daughters of Chinese merchants. One of the clan members, {{ill|Munakata Tokuyoshi|ja|宗形徳善|12=draft}}, offered his daughter, {{ill|Amako no Iratsume|ja|尼子娘|12=draft}}, to Emperor {{ill|Tenmu|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=draft}} as a consort. Their first son, {{ill|Prince Takasaka|ja|高市皇子|12=draft}}, born in {{ill|Hakuchi|ja|白雉|12=draft}} 5 (654), played a crucial role in the {{ill|Jinshin War|ja|壬申の乱|12=draft}}, earning high honors and later becoming the {{ill|Daijō-daijin|ja|太政大臣|12=draft}}. {{ill|Prince Nagaya|ja|長屋王|12=draft}} was his son, and he also became an ancestor of the {{ill|Takashina clan|ja|高階氏|12=draft}}. By {{ill|Daido|ja|大同|12=draft}} 2 (807), Munakata Taisha was granted 74 households in tribute. In {{ill|Jōwa|ja|承和|12=draft}} 7 (840), it was promoted to {{ill|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従五位下|1=Junior Fifth Rank|lt=Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|12=draft}}, and later, in {{ill|Jōgan|ja|貞観|12=draft}} 1 (859), to {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft}}. Following the {{ill|Tengyō no Ran|ja|天慶の乱|12=draft}} in {{ill|Tengyō|ja|天慶|12=draft}} 4 (941), the shrine was further elevated to {{ill|Senior First Rank|ja|正一位|1=Senior First Rank|12=draft}}, the highest divine rank. By {{ill|Tengen|ja|天元|12=draft}} 2 (979), the position of {{ill|Ōmiya-shi|ja|大宮司|12=draft}} (High Priest) was formally established by the {{ill|Dajōkan|ja|太政官|12=draft}}. From the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|12=draft}} onward, the Munakata clan, which had inherited the title of High Priest, became warriors and established themselves as powerful {{ill|kokujin lords|ja|国人領主|12=draft}}. However, during the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|12=draft}}, they were drawn into conflicts between the {{ill|Ōuchi clan|ja|大内氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtomo clan|ja|大友氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Shōni clan|ja|少弐氏|12=draft}}, leading to Munakata Taisha becoming a target of military attacks. The shrine suffered multiple instances of arson and destruction, and the Munakata clan gradually declined. Nonetheless, with continued reverence from the {{ill|imperial court|ja|朝廷|12=draft}} and the {{ill|samurai|ja|武家|12=draft}}, it was repeatedly rebuilt. The present Hetsu Shrine {{ill|honden|ja|本殿|12=draft}} with its beautiful {{ill|Kokerabuki|ja|こけら葺き|12=draft}} thatched roof was reconstructed in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 6 (1578) by the High Priest {{ill|Munakata Ujisada|ja|宗像氏貞|12=draft}}, while the {{ill|haiden|ja|拝殿|12=draft}} was rebuilt in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 16 (1590) by {{ill|Kobayakawa Takakage|ja|小早川隆景|12=draft}}, the ruler of Chikuzen. Both structures are now designated {{ill|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ja|重要文化財|12=draft}}. After the decline of the Munakata clan, the {{ill|Kusakari clan|ja|草刈氏|12=draft}}, including {{ill|Kusakari Shigetsugu|ja|草刈重継|12=draft}}, succeeded their role in shrine rituals. During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏|12=draft}}, lords of Chikuzen, repeatedly funded shrine reconstructions and land donations. Following the anti-Buddhist {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|12=draft}} policies in the late {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft}}, Munakata Taisha was separated from its associated {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Chinkoku-ji|ja|鎮国寺|12=draft}}. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 4 (1871), under the {{ill|modern shrine ranking system|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=draft}}, Munakata Shrine was classified as a {{ill|National Middle Shrine|ja|国幣中社|12=draft}}, before being promoted to {{ill|Imperial Middle Shrine|ja|官幣中社|12=draft}} on April 22 the following year. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 34 (1901), it was further elevated to {{ill|Imperial Grand Shrine|ja|官幣大社|12=draft}}, the highest rank. After {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}, the shrine grounds, which had fallen into disrepair, were restored thanks to donations from businessman {{ill|Idemitsu Sazō|ja|出光佐三|12=draft}}, a native of Munakata. He also played a crucial role in advocating for national research and excavation of the Okinoshima ritual site. ==See also== *[[Itsukushima Shrine]] which was dedicated to the same goddesses *[[Munakata Saikaku]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (archaeological materials)]] *[[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Munakata-taisha}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese mythology]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Munakata Taisha]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Munakata, Fukuoka]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:Munakata Shrines]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] [[Category:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Fixed Kofun templates]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[ja:宗像大社]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[en:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] {{Kofun navbar}} [[Category:New]]

These ''[[kami]]'' are believed to be daughters of the goddess [[Amaterasu]], the ancestress of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial family]] or to be the daughters of [[Susanoo]], who has also been worshipped there for many years as the god of mariners, and he has come to be worshipped as the god of traffic safety on land as well. Munakata Taisha is also home to many Japanese treasures. Hetsu-gū's ''[[honden]]'' (main shrine) and ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' (main prayer hall) are both designated [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Properties]] and the precincts are a [[Monuments of Japan|Historic Site]].{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/2661 |title=宗像神社境内 |trans-title=Munakata Jinja Precinct |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=15 June 2012}} The {{Nihongo|Shinpō-kan|神寶館}}, the shrine's treasure hall located on the east corner of Hetsu-gū's grounds, houses many important relics including six [[National Treasures of Japan]]. Over 120,000 artifacts housed in the Shinpō-kan were unearthed on [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]].{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |title=Stroll through Munakata History |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081013024006/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |archive-date=2008-10-13}} It was formerly an imperial shrine of the first rank (官幣大社, ''kanpei taisha'') in the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft}} refers collectively to the three shrines: '''Okitsu Shrine''' (沖津宮) on [[Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|Okinoshima]], '''Nakatsu Shrine''' (中津宮) on {{ill|Ōshima (Fukuoka)|ja|筑前大島|Ōshima (Fukuoka)=Ōshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Chikuzen Ōshima|12=draft}}, and the main shrine, '''Hetsu Shrine''' (辺津宮) in {{ill|Munakata, Fukuoka|ja|宗像市|12=draft}} Tajima. However, in modern usage, "Munakata Taisha" often refers only to Hetsu Shrine. Locally, Hetsu Shrine is known as "Tajima-sama" (田島さま). Nakatsu Shrine has a remote {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship site|12=draft}} for Okitsu Shrine called '''Etsu Shrine''' (瀛津宮) on Chikuzen Ōshima. Geographically, Nakatsu Shrine is 11 km from Hetsu Shrine, and Okitsu Shrine is another 49 km away, all aligned in a straight line. As one of the oldest shrines in Japan, Munakata Taisha is mentioned in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, and has been historically significant due to its location along the sea routes connecting Japan to the continent and the Korean Peninsula. Traditionally revered as a protector of maritime and travel safety, it continues to be widely worshiped today as the guardian deity of all roads, under the name {{ill|Three_Munakata_Goddesses|lt=Dōshunomikoto|ja|道主貴|12=draft}}. Consequently, in Fukuoka Prefecture and surrounding areas, it is common to see cars displaying Munakata Taisha {{ill|stickers|ja|シール|12=draft}}, and many people visit the shrine's prayer hall to have their new vehicles blessed. Additionally, the concept of a vehicle-mounted traffic safety {{ill|Omamori|ja|お守り|12=draft}} is said to have originated at Munakata Taisha. {{ill|Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Okinoshima|ja|沖ノ島|12=draft}}, where Okitsu Shrine is located, has long been a key maritime transit point. Since ancient times, it has been considered forbidden to disclose anything seen or heard on the island, leading to its moniker "Ofugen-sama" (お不言さま, "The Island of Silence"). The entire island is regarded as a sacred body, and to this day, women are prohibited from setting foot on it, while men must undergo a {{ill|Misogi|ja|禊|12=draft}} purification ritual before landing. Some criticize this as gender discrimination, but a traditional belief states that the island's deity, {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|田心姫神|12=draft}}, is a female kami who would grow jealous and curse any woman who set foot there. However, the accuracy of this explanation is uncertain. Archaeological excavations of Okinoshima, conducted over more than a decade since 1954, uncovered numerous ancient ritual sites and offerings dating from the 4th to 9th centuries, including decorated artifacts, as well as stone tools and pottery from the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代|12=draft}} and {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft}}. Due to this wealth of artifacts, the island is often referred to as the "Marine {{ill|Shōsōin|ja|正倉院|12=draft}}." These discoveries suggest that Okinoshima has been a religious center for maritime people since prehistoric times. Today, the island is designated as a safe harbor for emergency shelter during typhoons. A {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft}} plaque displayed in the main shrine hall was personally inscribed by {{ill|Prince Fushimi Sadanaru|ja|伏見宮貞愛親王|12=draft}}, while the "Munakata Shrine" plaque was written by imperial envoy {{ill|Hamaguchi Akitaka|ja|葉室顕孝|12=draft}}, a {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft}} Gon Dainagon. In 2009, an initiative led by [[:ja:Sakuji Yoshimura|Sakuji Yoshimura]], an [[Egyptologist]], proposed designating Okinoshima and related Munakata heritage sites as a {{ill|lt=UNESCO World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site|ja|世界遺産|12=draft}}. That year, "Okitsu Shrine, Nakatsu Shrine, and Hetsu Shrine," along with "Okitsu Shrine {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=Worship Site|12=draft}} and all of Okinoshima," were added to Japan's tentative list under the title "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region." In 2015, it was officially nominated, and on July 2017, during the {{ill|UNESCO World Heritage Committee|ja|ユネスコ世界遺産委員会|12=draft}} session in {{ill|Kraków|ja|クラクフ|12=draft}}, {{ill|Poland|ja|ポーランド|12=draft}}, the site was officially inscribed as a World Heritage Site. ==Three shrines== [[File:Shimmon Gate of Munakata Grand Shrine (Hetsu Shrine) 2.JPG|thumb|250px|Gate of Hetsu-no-miya]] All three shrines are located in Fukuoka Prefecture, yet they are all on separate islands. The main shrine, Hetsu-gū, is located on the mainland of [[Kyūshū]]. Nakatsu-gū is established at the foot of Mt. Mitake on the island of [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] off the west coast of Kyūshū.{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ejx2.html |title=Munakata-taisha Nakatsu-gu Shrine |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=[[Japan National Tourist Organization]]}} The final shrine, Okitsu-gū, is on the island of [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] located in the middle of the [[Genkai Sea]]. The shrine occupies the entire island, therefore women are not allowed to set foot on the island and men must perform a [[misogi|purification ceremony]] before landing.{{cite web |url=http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |access-date=2008-06-02 |title=Muna Kata Tai Sha |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060125084824/http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |archive-date=2006-01-25}} In 2009 the three shrines were submitted for future inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage List]] as part of the serial nomination [[Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region]].{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5400/ |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=15 June 2012}}{{cite web |url=http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=World Heritage Promotion Committee of "Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region" |access-date=15 June 2012 |archive-date=5 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105154558/http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |title=Overview of Munakata City |access-date=2008-06-03 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829224830/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |archive-date=2010-08-29}} In July, 2017 Japan's Okinoshima Island gained UNESCO World Heritage Status.{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-40549909 |title=Japan's Okinoshima island gains Unesco World Heritage status |date=2017-07-09 |work=BBC News |access-date=2017-07-09 |language=en-GB}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! Shrine Name ! Enshrined deity ! Island location ! Coordinates |- | {{Nihongo|'''Hetsu-gū'''|辺津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ichikishimahime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|12=draft}}|市杵島姫神}} | [[Kyūshū]] | {{coord|33|49|53|N|130|30|50|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1100}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Nakatsu-gū'''|中津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|12=draft}}|湍津姫神}} | [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] | {{coord|33|53|49|N|130|25|56|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Okitsu-gū'''|沖津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|12=draft}}|田心姫神}} | [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] | {{coord|34|14|33|N|130|6|14|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |} [[File:Children born from the Challenge of Amaterasu and Susanoo-en.svg|thumb|240x240px|The three shrines correspond to the three daughters of Susanoo shown on the left]] == History == According to {{ill|tradition|ja|伝承|12=draft}}, the origins of {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft}} trace back to {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話|12=draft}}. During the {{ill|Oath of Amaterasu and Susanoo|ja|アマテラスとスサノオの誓約|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|12=draft}} shattered {{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft}}’s sword with her teeth and blew out fragments, from which the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|12=draft}} were born. The goddesses, carrying Amaterasu’s {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft}}, descended to the islands of Munakata floating in the Genkai Sea along the northern sea route to protect and aid her grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ja|ニニギノミコト|12=draft}}, establishing the origins of Munakata Taisha. In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft}}, the only deities described as descending from the heavens before Ninigi-no-Mikoto’s {{ill|descent of the heavenly grandchild|ja|天孫降臨|12=draft}} are the Three Munakata Goddesses. This makes their recorded descent and enshrinement one of the earliest explicitly documented in the chronicles. Regarding the sacred objects representing the Three Munakata Goddesses, the {{ill|Chikuzen Province|ja|筑前国|12=draft}} {{ill|Fudoki|ja|風土記|12=draft}} states in its surviving fragments: {{quote|“According to the Saikaidō Fudoki, when the Munakata Great Deity descended from the heavens to settle at Sakimotoyama, a blue gem was placed at Okitsu Shrine, an eight-span purple gem at Nakatsu Shrine, and an eight-span mirror at Hetsu Shrine. These three objects became the forms of the deities and were enshrined in the three shrines. This tradition was later obscured, and the area was renamed ‘Munakata.’ The descendants of the deity, the Munakata clan, are the present-day Munakata Ason.”}} In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft}}, the name "Munakata" is written as "Mune-Kata" (胸形), and also appears as "Munakata" (宗形) or "Mune-Kata" (胸肩). Some theories suggest that it originally referred to a water lagoon. Munakata Taisha was revered as the clan deity of the local people. It is said that when {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后|12=draft}} prayed for safe passage during her {{ill|conquest of the Three Han|ja|三韓征伐|12=draft}}, she experienced divine miracles, leading to the tradition of dispatching envoys to Munakata for rituals on significant occasions. Due to its importance, the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=draft}} honored the shrine, and each time the imperial capital was relocated, its deity was enshrined in the {{ill|Kashiko-dokoro|ja|賢所|12=draft}}, the imperial sanctuary. This highlights the deity’s reputation as a protector of maritime safety. With the introduction of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft}}, Munakata was designated as a {{ill|shrine territory|ja|寺社領|12=draft}}, and the {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|1=Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|12=draft}}, a local ruling family, served as high priests while also governing the {{ill|shrine district|ja|神郡|12=draft}}. According to an inscription on a stone monument recording the lineage of the Munakata clan, two generations of their chieftains married daughters of Chinese merchants. One of the clan members, {{ill|Munakata Tokuyoshi|ja|宗形徳善|12=draft}}, offered his daughter, {{ill|Amako no Iratsume|ja|尼子娘|12=draft}}, to Emperor {{ill|Tenmu|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=draft}} as a consort. Their first son, {{ill|Prince Takasaka|ja|高市皇子|12=draft}}, born in {{ill|Hakuchi|ja|白雉|12=draft}} 5 (654), played a crucial role in the {{ill|Jinshin War|ja|壬申の乱|12=draft}}, earning high honors and later becoming the {{ill|Daijō-daijin|ja|太政大臣|12=draft}}. {{ill|Prince Nagaya|ja|長屋王|12=draft}} was his son, and he also became an ancestor of the {{ill|Takashina clan|ja|高階氏|12=draft}}. By {{ill|Daido|ja|大同|12=draft}} 2 (807), Munakata Taisha was granted 74 households in tribute. In {{ill|Jōwa|ja|承和|12=draft}} 7 (840), it was promoted to {{ill|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従五位下|1=Junior Fifth Rank|lt=Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|12=draft}}, and later, in {{ill|Jōgan|ja|貞観|12=draft}} 1 (859), to {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft}}. Following the {{ill|Tengyō no Ran|ja|天慶の乱|12=draft}} in {{ill|Tengyō|ja|天慶|12=draft}} 4 (941), the shrine was further elevated to {{ill|Senior First Rank|ja|正一位|1=Senior First Rank|12=draft}}, the highest divine rank. By {{ill|Tengen|ja|天元|12=draft}} 2 (979), the position of {{ill|Ōmiya-shi|ja|大宮司|12=draft}} (High Priest) was formally established by the {{ill|Dajōkan|ja|太政官|12=draft}}. From the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|12=draft}} onward, the Munakata clan, which had inherited the title of High Priest, became warriors and established themselves as powerful {{ill|kokujin lords|ja|国人領主|12=draft}}. However, during the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|12=draft}}, they were drawn into conflicts between the {{ill|Ōuchi clan|ja|大内氏|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtomo clan|ja|大友氏|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Shōni clan|ja|少弐氏|12=draft}}, leading to Munakata Taisha becoming a target of military attacks. The shrine suffered multiple instances of arson and destruction, and the Munakata clan gradually declined. Nonetheless, with continued reverence from the {{ill|imperial court|ja|朝廷|12=draft}} and the {{ill|samurai|ja|武家|12=draft}}, it was repeatedly rebuilt. The present Hetsu Shrine {{ill|honden|ja|本殿|12=draft}} with its beautiful {{ill|Kokerabuki|ja|こけら葺き|12=draft}} thatched roof was reconstructed in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 6 (1578) by the High Priest {{ill|Munakata Ujisada|ja|宗像氏貞|12=draft}}, while the {{ill|haiden|ja|拝殿|12=draft}} was rebuilt in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft}} 16 (1590) by {{ill|Kobayakawa Takakage|ja|小早川隆景|12=draft}}, the ruler of Chikuzen. Both structures are now designated {{ill|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ja|重要文化財|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)|2=ja|3=重要文化財|lt=Important Cultural Property|qq= (Japan)|4=ko|5=일본의_중요문화재|12=draft}}. After the decline of the Munakata clan, the {{ill|Kusakari clan|ja|草刈氏|12=draft}}, including {{ill|Kusakari Shigetsugu|ja|草刈重継|12=draft}}, succeeded their role in shrine rituals. During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏|12=draft}}, lords of Chikuzen, repeatedly funded shrine reconstructions and land donations. Following the anti-Buddhist {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|12=draft}} policies in the late {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft}}, Munakata Taisha was separated from its associated {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Chinkoku-ji|ja|鎮国寺|12=draft}}. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 4 (1871), under the {{ill|modern shrine ranking system|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=draft}}, Munakata Shrine was classified as a {{ill|National Middle Shrine|ja|国幣中社|12=draft}}, before being promoted to {{ill|Imperial Middle Shrine|ja|官幣中社|12=draft}} on April 22 the following year. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft}} 34 (1901), it was further elevated to {{ill|Imperial Grand Shrine|ja|官幣大社|12=draft}}, the highest rank. After {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft}}, the shrine grounds, which had fallen into disrepair, were restored thanks to donations from businessman {{ill|Idemitsu Sazō|ja|出光佐三|12=draft}}, a native of Munakata. He also played a crucial role in advocating for national research and excavation of the Okinoshima ritual site. ==See also== *[[Itsukushima Shrine]] which was dedicated to the same goddesses *[[Munakata Saikaku]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (archaeological materials)]] *[[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Munakata-taisha}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] {{draft categories| [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese mythology]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Munakata Taisha]][[Category:qq]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Munakata, Fukuoka]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:Munakata Shrines]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] [[Category:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Fixed Kofun templates]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[ja:宗像大社]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[en:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] {{Kofun navbar}} [[Category:New]]

Fukuoka 〒811-3701 | website = {{URL|http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Munakata Taisha'''|宗像大社}} is a collection of three [[Shinto]] [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] located in [[Munakata, Fukuoka|Munakata]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the head of the approximately 6,000 Munakata shrines all over the country. Although the name Munakata Taisha refers to all three shrines—Hetsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū—it is commonly used to refer to Hetsu-gū alone. However, in modern usage, "Munakata Taisha" often refers only to Hetsu Shrine. Locally, Hetsu Shrine is known as "Tajima-sama" (田島さま). Nakatsu Shrine has a remote {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship site|12=draft|12=draft}} for Okitsu Shrine called '''Etsu Shrine''' (瀛津宮) on Chikuzen Ōshima. Geographically, Nakatsu Shrine is 11 km from Hetsu Shrine, and Okitsu Shrine is another 49 km away, all aligned in a straight line. As one of the oldest shrines in Japan, Munakata Taisha is mentioned in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, and has been historically significant due to its location along the sea routes connecting Japan to the continent and the Korean Peninsula. Traditionally revered as a protector of maritime and travel safety, it continues to be widely worshiped today as the guardian deity of all roads, under the name {{ill|Three_Munakata_Goddesses|lt=Dōshunomikoto|ja|道主貴|12=draft|12=draft}}. Consequently, in Fukuoka Prefecture and surrounding areas, it is common to see cars displaying Munakata Taisha {{ill|stickers|ja|シール|12=draft|12=draft}}, and many people visit the shrine's prayer hall to have their new vehicles blessed. Additionally, the concept of a vehicle-mounted traffic safety {{ill|Omamori|ja|お守り|12=draft|12=draft}} is said to have originated at Munakata Taisha. {{ill|Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Okinoshima|ja|沖ノ島|12=draft|12=draft}}, where Okitsu Shrine is located, has long been a key maritime transit point. Since ancient times, it has been considered forbidden to disclose anything seen or heard on the island, leading to its moniker "Ofugen-sama" (お不言さま, "The Island of Silence"). The entire island is regarded as a sacred body, and to this day, women are prohibited from setting foot on it, while men must undergo a {{ill|Misogi|ja|禊|12=draft|12=draft}} purification ritual before landing. Some criticize this as gender discrimination, but a traditional belief states that the island's deity, {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|田心姫神|12=draft|12=draft}}, is a female kami who would grow jealous and curse any woman who set foot there. However, the accuracy of this explanation is uncertain. Archaeological excavations of Okinoshima, conducted over more than a decade since 1954, uncovered numerous ancient ritual sites and offerings dating from the 4th to 9th centuries, including decorated artifacts, as well as stone tools and pottery from the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft|12=draft}}. Due to this wealth of artifacts, the island is often referred to as the "Marine {{ill|Shōsōin|ja|正倉院|12=draft|12=draft}}." These discoveries suggest that Okinoshima has been a religious center for maritime people since prehistoric times. Today, the island is designated as a safe harbor for emergency shelter during typhoons. A {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft|12=draft}} plaque displayed in the main shrine hall was personally inscribed by {{ill|Prince Fushimi Sadanaru|ja|伏見宮貞愛親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, while the "Munakata Shrine" plaque was written by imperial envoy {{ill|Hamaguchi Akitaka|ja|葉室顕孝|12=draft|12=draft}}, a {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}} Gon Dainagon. In 2009, an initiative led by [[:ja:Sakuji Yoshimura|Sakuji Yoshimura]], an [[Egyptologist]], proposed designating Okinoshima and related Munakata heritage sites as a {{ill|lt=UNESCO World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site|ja|世界遺産|12=draft|12=draft}}. That year, "Okitsu Shrine, Nakatsu Shrine, and Hetsu Shrine," along with "Okitsu Shrine {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=Worship Site|12=draft|12=draft}} and all of Okinoshima," were added to Japan's tentative list under the title "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region." In 2015, it was officially nominated, and on July 2017, during the {{ill|UNESCO World Heritage Committee|ja|ユネスコ世界遺産委員会|12=draft|12=draft}} session in {{ill|Kraków|ja|クラクフ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Poland|ja|ポーランド|12=draft|12=draft}}, the site was officially inscribed as a World Heritage Site. ==Three shrines== [[File:Shimmon Gate of Munakata Grand Shrine (Hetsu Shrine) 2.JPG|thumb|250px|Gate of Hetsu-no-miya]] All three shrines are located in Fukuoka Prefecture, yet they are all on separate islands. The main shrine, Hetsu-gū, is located on the mainland of [[Kyūshū]]. Nakatsu-gū is established at the foot of Mt. Mitake on the island of [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] off the west coast of Kyūshū.{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ejx2.html |title=Munakata-taisha Nakatsu-gu Shrine |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=[[Japan National Tourist Organization]]}} The final shrine, Okitsu-gū, is on the island of [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] located in the middle of the [[Genkai Sea]]. The shrine occupies the entire island, therefore women are not allowed to set foot on the island and men must perform a [[misogi|purification ceremony]] before landing.{{cite web |url=http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |access-date=2008-06-02 |title=Muna Kata Tai Sha |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060125084824/http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |archive-date=2006-01-25}} In 2009 the three shrines were submitted for future inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage List]] as part of the serial nomination [[Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region]].{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5400/ |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=15 June 2012}}{{cite web |url=http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=World Heritage Promotion Committee of "Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region" |access-date=15 June 2012 |archive-date=5 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105154558/http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |title=Overview of Munakata City |access-date=2008-06-03 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829224830/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |archive-date=2010-08-29}} In July, 2017 Japan's Okinoshima Island gained UNESCO World Heritage Status.{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-40549909 |title=Japan's Okinoshima island gains Unesco World Heritage status |date=2017-07-09 |work=BBC News |access-date=2017-07-09 |language=en-GB}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! Coordinates |- | {{Nihongo|'''Hetsu-gū'''|辺津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ichikishimahime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|市杵島姫神}} | [[Kyūshū]] | {{coord|33|49|53|N|130|30|50|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1100}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Nakatsu-gū'''|中津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|湍津姫神}} | [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] | {{coord|33|53|49|N|130|25|56|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Okitsu-gū'''|沖津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|田心姫神}} | [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] | {{coord|34|14|33|N|130|6|14|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |} [[File:Children born from the Challenge of Amaterasu and Susanoo-en.svg|thumb|240x240px|The three shrines correspond to the three daughters of Susanoo shown on the left]] == History == According to {{ill|tradition|ja|伝承|12=draft|12=draft}}, the origins of {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft|12=draft}} trace back to {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話|12=draft|12=draft}}. During the {{ill|Oath of Amaterasu and Susanoo|ja|アマテラスとスサノオの誓約|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|12=draft|12=draft}} shattered {{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft|12=draft}}’s sword with her teeth and blew out fragments, from which the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|12=draft|12=draft}} were born. The goddesses, carrying Amaterasu’s {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft|12=draft}}, descended to the islands of Munakata floating in the Genkai Sea along the northern sea route to protect and aid her grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ja|ニニギノミコト|12=draft|12=draft}}, establishing the origins of Munakata Taisha. In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, the only deities described as descending from the heavens before Ninigi-no-Mikoto’s {{ill|descent of the heavenly grandchild|ja|天孫降臨|12=draft|12=draft}} are the Three Munakata Goddesses. This makes their recorded descent and enshrinement one of the earliest explicitly documented in the chronicles. Regarding the sacred objects representing the Three Munakata Goddesses, the {{ill|Chikuzen Province|ja|筑前国|12=draft|12=draft}} {{ill|Fudoki|ja|風土記|12=draft|12=draft}} states in its surviving fragments: {{quote|“According to the Saikaidō Fudoki, when the Munakata Great Deity descended from the heavens to settle at Sakimotoyama, a blue gem was placed at Okitsu Shrine, an eight-span purple gem at Nakatsu Shrine, and an eight-span mirror at Hetsu Shrine. These three objects became the forms of the deities and were enshrined in the three shrines. This tradition was later obscured, and the area was renamed ‘Munakata.’ The descendants of the deity, the Munakata clan, are the present-day Munakata Ason.”}} In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}}, the name "Munakata" is written as "Mune-Kata" (胸形), and also appears as "Munakata" (宗形) or "Mune-Kata" (胸肩). Some theories suggest that it originally referred to a water lagoon. Munakata Taisha was revered as the clan deity of the local people. It is said that when {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后|12=draft|12=draft}} prayed for safe passage during her {{ill|conquest of the Three Han|ja|三韓征伐|12=draft|12=draft}}, she experienced divine miracles, leading to the tradition of dispatching envoys to Munakata for rituals on significant occasions. Due to its importance, the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=draft|12=draft}} honored the shrine, and each time the imperial capital was relocated, its deity was enshrined in the {{ill|Kashiko-dokoro|ja|賢所|12=draft|12=draft}}, the imperial sanctuary. This highlights the deity’s reputation as a protector of maritime safety. With the introduction of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata was designated as a {{ill|shrine territory|ja|寺社領|12=draft|12=draft}}, and the {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|1=Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|12=draft|12=draft}}, a local ruling family, served as high priests while also governing the {{ill|shrine district|ja|神郡|12=draft|12=draft}}. According to an inscription on a stone monument recording the lineage of the Munakata clan, two generations of their chieftains married daughters of Chinese merchants. One of the clan members, {{ill|Munakata Tokuyoshi|ja|宗形徳善|12=draft|12=draft}}, offered his daughter, {{ill|Amako no Iratsume|ja|尼子娘|12=draft|12=draft}}, to Emperor {{ill|Tenmu|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=draft|12=draft}} as a consort. Their first son, {{ill|Prince Takasaka|ja|高市皇子|12=draft|12=draft}}, born in {{ill|Hakuchi|ja|白雉|12=draft|12=draft}} 5 (654), played a crucial role in the {{ill|Jinshin War|ja|壬申の乱|12=draft|12=draft}}, earning high honors and later becoming the {{ill|Daijō-daijin|ja|太政大臣|12=draft|12=draft}}. {{ill|Prince Nagaya|ja|長屋王|12=draft|12=draft}} was his son, and he also became an ancestor of the {{ill|Takashina clan|ja|高階氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. By {{ill|Daido|ja|大同|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 (807), Munakata Taisha was granted 74 households in tribute. In {{ill|Jōwa|ja|承和|12=draft|12=draft}} 7 (840), it was promoted to {{ill|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従五位下|1=Junior Fifth Rank|lt=Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|12=draft|12=draft}}, and later, in {{ill|Jōgan|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} 1 (859), to {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}}. Following the {{ill|Tengyō no Ran|ja|天慶の乱|12=draft|12=draft}} in {{ill|Tengyō|ja|天慶|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 (941), the shrine was further elevated to {{ill|Senior First Rank|ja|正一位|1=Senior First Rank|12=draft|12=draft}}, the highest divine rank. By {{ill|Tengen|ja|天元|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 (979), the position of {{ill|Ōmiya-shi|ja|大宮司|12=draft|12=draft}} (High Priest) was formally established by the {{ill|Dajōkan|ja|太政官|12=draft|12=draft}}. From the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|12=draft|12=draft}} onward, the Munakata clan, which had inherited the title of High Priest, became warriors and established themselves as powerful {{ill|kokujin lords|ja|国人領主|12=draft|12=draft}}. However, during the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, they were drawn into conflicts between the {{ill|Ōuchi clan|ja|大内氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtomo clan|ja|大友氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Shōni clan|ja|少弐氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, leading to Munakata Taisha becoming a target of military attacks. The shrine suffered multiple instances of arson and destruction, and the Munakata clan gradually declined. Nonetheless, with continued reverence from the {{ill|imperial court|ja|朝廷|12=draft|12=draft}} and the {{ill|samurai|ja|武家|12=draft|12=draft}}, it was repeatedly rebuilt. The present Hetsu Shrine {{ill|honden|ja|本殿|12=draft|12=draft}} with its beautiful {{ill|Kokerabuki|ja|こけら葺き|12=draft|12=draft}} thatched roof was reconstructed in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 6 (1578) by the High Priest {{ill|Munakata Ujisada|ja|宗像氏貞|12=draft|12=draft}}, while the {{ill|haiden|ja|拝殿|12=draft|12=draft}} was rebuilt in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 16 (1590) by {{ill|Kobayakawa Takakage|ja|小早川隆景|12=draft|12=draft}}, the ruler of Chikuzen. Both structures are now designated {{ill|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ja|重要文化財|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)|2=ja|3=重要文化財|lt=Important Cultural Property|qq= (Japan)|4=ko|5=일본의_중요문화재|12=draft|12=draft}}. After the decline of the Munakata clan, the {{ill|Kusakari clan|ja|草刈氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, including {{ill|Kusakari Shigetsugu|ja|草刈重継|12=draft|12=draft}}, succeeded their role in shrine rituals. During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, lords of Chikuzen, repeatedly funded shrine reconstructions and land donations. Following the anti-Buddhist {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|12=draft|12=draft}} policies in the late {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata Taisha was separated from its associated {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|12=draft|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Chinkoku-ji|ja|鎮国寺|12=draft|12=draft}}. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 (1871), under the {{ill|modern shrine ranking system|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata Shrine was classified as a {{ill|National Middle Shrine|ja|国幣中社|12=draft|12=draft}}, before being promoted to {{ill|Imperial Middle Shrine|ja|官幣中社|12=draft|12=draft}} on April 22 the following year. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 34 (1901), it was further elevated to {{ill|Imperial Grand Shrine|ja|官幣大社|12=draft|12=draft}}, the highest rank. After {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}, the shrine grounds, which had fallen into disrepair, were restored thanks to donations from businessman {{ill|Idemitsu Sazō|ja|出光佐三|12=draft|12=draft}}, a native of Munakata. He also played a crucial role in advocating for national research and excavation of the Okinoshima ritual site. ==See also== *[[Itsukushima Shrine]] which was dedicated to the same goddesses *[[Munakata Saikaku]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (archaeological materials)]] *[[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Munakata-taisha}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{draft categories| }} {{Kofun navbar}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese mythology]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Munakata, Fukuoka]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:Munakata Shrines]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] [[Category:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Fixed Kofun templates]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[ja:宗像大社]] [[en:Munakata Taisha]]

Fukuoka 〒811-3701 | website = {{URL|http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Munakata Taisha'''|宗像大社}} is a collection of three [[Shinto]] [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] located in [[Munakata, Fukuoka|Munakata]], [[Fukuoka Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It is the head of the approximately 6,000 Munakata shrines all over the country. Although the name Munakata Taisha refers to all three shrines—Hetsu-gū, Nakatsu-gū and Okitsu-gū—it is commonly used to refer to Hetsu-gū alone. As documented in Japan's second oldest book, ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'', the shrines are devoted to the {{Nihongo|three Munakata goddesses|宗像三女神|Munakata-sanjojin}}. These ''[[kami]]'' are believed to be daughters of the goddess [[Amaterasu]], the ancestress of the [[Imperial House of Japan|imperial family]] or to be the daughters of [[Susanoo]], who has also been worshipped there for many years as the god of mariners, and he has come to be worshipped as the god of traffic safety on land as well. Munakata Taisha is also home to many Japanese treasures. Hetsu-gū's ''[[honden]]'' (main shrine) and ''[[haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' (main prayer hall) are both designated [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Properties]] and the precincts are a [[Monuments of Japan|Historic Site]].{{cite web |url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/401/2661 |title=宗像神社境内 |trans-title=Munakata Jinja Precinct |publisher=[[Agency for Cultural Affairs]] |access-date=15 June 2012}} The {{Nihongo|Shinpō-kan|神寶館}}, the shrine's treasure hall located on the east corner of Hetsu-gū's grounds, houses many important relics including six [[National Treasures of Japan]]. Over 120,000 artifacts housed in the Shinpō-kan were unearthed on [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]].{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |title=Stroll through Munakata History |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081013024006/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/sumouyo03.html |archive-date=2008-10-13}} It was formerly an imperial shrine of the first rank (官幣大社, ''kanpei taisha'') in the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]]. == Overview == {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft|12=draft}} refers collectively to the three shrines: '''Okitsu Shrine''' (沖津宮) on [[Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|Okinoshima]], '''Nakatsu Shrine''' (中津宮) on {{ill|Ōshima (Fukuoka)|ja|筑前大島|Ōshima (Fukuoka)=Ōshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Chikuzen Ōshima|12=draft|12=draft}}, and the main shrine, '''Hetsu Shrine''' (辺津宮) in {{ill|Munakata, Fukuoka|ja|宗像市|12=draft|12=draft}} Tajima. However, in modern usage, "Munakata Taisha" often refers only to Hetsu Shrine. Locally, Hetsu Shrine is known as "Tajima-sama" (田島さま). Nakatsu Shrine has a remote {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship site|12=draft|12=draft}} for Okitsu Shrine called '''Etsu Shrine''' (瀛津宮) on Chikuzen Ōshima. Geographically, Nakatsu Shrine is 11 km from Hetsu Shrine, and Okitsu Shrine is another 49 km away, all aligned in a straight line. As one of the oldest shrines in Japan, Munakata Taisha is mentioned in the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, and has been historically significant due to its location along the sea routes connecting Japan to the continent and the Korean Peninsula. Traditionally revered as a protector of maritime and travel safety, it continues to be widely worshiped today as the guardian deity of all roads, under the name {{ill|Three_Munakata_Goddesses|lt=Dōshunomikoto|ja|道主貴|12=draft|12=draft}}. Consequently, in Fukuoka Prefecture and surrounding areas, it is common to see cars displaying Munakata Taisha {{ill|stickers|ja|シール|12=draft|12=draft}}, and many people visit the shrine's prayer hall to have their new vehicles blessed. Additionally, the concept of a vehicle-mounted traffic safety {{ill|Omamori|ja|お守り|12=draft|12=draft}} is said to have originated at Munakata Taisha. {{ill|Okinoshima (Fukuoka)|lt=Okinoshima|ja|沖ノ島|12=draft|12=draft}}, where Okitsu Shrine is located, has long been a key maritime transit point. Since ancient times, it has been considered forbidden to disclose anything seen or heard on the island, leading to its moniker "Ofugen-sama" (お不言さま, "The Island of Silence"). The entire island is regarded as a sacred body, and to this day, women are prohibited from setting foot on it, while men must undergo a {{ill|Misogi|ja|禊|12=draft|12=draft}} purification ritual before landing. Some criticize this as gender discrimination, but a traditional belief states that the island's deity, {{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|田心姫神|12=draft|12=draft}}, is a female kami who would grow jealous and curse any woman who set foot there. However, the accuracy of this explanation is uncertain. Archaeological excavations of Okinoshima, conducted over more than a decade since 1954, uncovered numerous ancient ritual sites and offerings dating from the 4th to 9th centuries, including decorated artifacts, as well as stone tools and pottery from the {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代|12=draft|12=draft}}. Due to this wealth of artifacts, the island is often referred to as the "Marine {{ill|Shōsōin|ja|正倉院|12=draft|12=draft}}." These discoveries suggest that Okinoshima has been a religious center for maritime people since prehistoric times. Today, the island is designated as a safe harbor for emergency shelter during typhoons. A {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft|12=draft}} plaque displayed in the main shrine hall was personally inscribed by {{ill|Prince Fushimi Sadanaru|ja|伏見宮貞愛親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, while the "Munakata Shrine" plaque was written by imperial envoy {{ill|Hamaguchi Akitaka|ja|葉室顕孝|12=draft|12=draft}}, a {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}} Gon Dainagon. In 2009, an initiative led by [[:ja:Sakuji Yoshimura|Sakuji Yoshimura]], an [[Egyptologist]], proposed designating Okinoshima and related Munakata heritage sites as a {{ill|lt=UNESCO World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site|ja|世界遺産|12=draft|12=draft}}. That year, "Okitsu Shrine, Nakatsu Shrine, and Hetsu Shrine," along with "Okitsu Shrine {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=Worship Site|12=draft|12=draft}} and all of Okinoshima," were added to Japan's tentative list under the title "Sacred Island of Okinoshima and Associated Sites in the Munakata Region." In 2015, it was officially nominated, and on July 2017, during the {{ill|UNESCO World Heritage Committee|ja|ユネスコ世界遺産委員会|12=draft|12=draft}} session in {{ill|Kraków|ja|クラクフ|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Poland|ja|ポーランド|12=draft|12=draft}}, the site was officially inscribed as a World Heritage Site. ==Three shrines== [[File:Shimmon Gate of Munakata Grand Shrine (Hetsu Shrine) 2.JPG|thumb|250px|Gate of Hetsu-no-miya]] All three shrines are located in Fukuoka Prefecture, yet they are all on separate islands. The main shrine, Hetsu-gū, is located on the mainland of [[Kyūshū]]. Nakatsu-gū is established at the foot of Mt. Mitake on the island of [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] off the west coast of Kyūshū.{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ejx2.html |title=Munakata-taisha Nakatsu-gu Shrine |access-date=2008-06-02 |work=[[Japan National Tourist Organization]]}} The final shrine, Okitsu-gū, is on the island of [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] located in the middle of the [[Genkai Sea]]. The shrine occupies the entire island, therefore women are not allowed to set foot on the island and men must perform a [[misogi|purification ceremony]] before landing.{{cite web |url=http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |access-date=2008-06-02 |title=Muna Kata Tai Sha |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060125084824/http://www.munakata-taisha.or.jp/e/ |archive-date=2006-01-25}} In 2009 the three shrines were submitted for future inscription on the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage List]] as part of the serial nomination [[Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region]].{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5400/ |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=15 June 2012}}{{cite web |url=http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |title=Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region |publisher=World Heritage Promotion Committee of "Okinoshima Island and Related Sites in Munakata Region" |access-date=15 June 2012 |archive-date=5 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161105154558/http://www.okinoshima-heritage.jp/en/introductions/okinoshima |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |title=Overview of Munakata City |access-date=2008-06-03 |work=宗像市公式Webサイト |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100829224830/http://www.city.munakata.lg.jp/e-shigai/yokatoko02.html |archive-date=2010-08-29}} In July, 2017 Japan's Okinoshima Island gained UNESCO World Heritage Status.{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-40549909 |title=Japan's Okinoshima island gains Unesco World Heritage status |date=2017-07-09 |work=BBC News |access-date=2017-07-09 |language=en-GB}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! Shrine Name ! Enshrined deity ! Island location ! Coordinates |- | {{Nihongo|'''Hetsu-gū'''|辺津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Ichikishimahime|ja|イチキシマヒメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|市杵島姫神}} | [[Kyūshū]] | {{coord|33|49|53|N|130|30|50|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1100}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Nakatsu-gū'''|中津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagitsuhime|ja|タギツヒメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|湍津姫神}} | [[Nii Ōshima|Ōshima]] | {{coord|33|53|49|N|130|25|56|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |- | {{Nihongo|'''Okitsu-gū'''|沖津宮}} | {{Nihongo|{{ill|Tagorihime|ja|タキリビメ|12=draft|12=draft}}|田心姫神}} | [[Okinoshima, Munakata|Okinoshima]] | {{coord|34|14|33|N|130|6|14|E|display=inline|region:JP_type:isle}} |} [[File:Children born from the Challenge of Amaterasu and Susanoo-en.svg|thumb|240x240px|The three shrines correspond to the three daughters of Susanoo shown on the left]] == History == According to {{ill|tradition|ja|伝承|12=draft|12=draft}}, the origins of {{ill|Munakata Taisha|ja|宗像大社|12=draft|12=draft}} trace back to {{ill|Japanese mythology|ja|日本神話|12=draft|12=draft}}. During the {{ill|Oath of Amaterasu and Susanoo|ja|アマテラスとスサノオの誓約|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|12=draft|12=draft}} shattered {{ill|Susanoo|ja|素戔嗚尊|12=draft|12=draft}}’s sword with her teeth and blew out fragments, from which the {{ill|Three Munakata Goddesses|ja|宗像三女神|1=Three Munakata Goddesses|12=draft|12=draft}} were born. The goddesses, carrying Amaterasu’s {{ill|divine decree|ja|神勅|12=draft|12=draft}}, descended to the islands of Munakata floating in the Genkai Sea along the northern sea route to protect and aid her grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|ja|ニニギノミコト|12=draft|12=draft}}, establishing the origins of Munakata Taisha. In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}} and {{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀|12=draft|12=draft}}, the only deities described as descending from the heavens before Ninigi-no-Mikoto’s {{ill|descent of the heavenly grandchild|ja|天孫降臨|12=draft|12=draft}} are the Three Munakata Goddesses. This makes their recorded descent and enshrinement one of the earliest explicitly documented in the chronicles. Regarding the sacred objects representing the Three Munakata Goddesses, the {{ill|Chikuzen Province|ja|筑前国|12=draft|12=draft}} {{ill|Fudoki|ja|風土記|12=draft|12=draft}} states in its surviving fragments: {{quote|“According to the Saikaidō Fudoki, when the Munakata Great Deity descended from the heavens to settle at Sakimotoyama, a blue gem was placed at Okitsu Shrine, an eight-span purple gem at Nakatsu Shrine, and an eight-span mirror at Hetsu Shrine. These three objects became the forms of the deities and were enshrined in the three shrines. This tradition was later obscured, and the area was renamed ‘Munakata.’ The descendants of the deity, the Munakata clan, are the present-day Munakata Ason.”}} In the {{ill|Kojiki|ja|古事記|12=draft|12=draft}}, the name "Munakata" is written as "Mune-Kata" (胸形), and also appears as "Munakata" (宗形) or "Mune-Kata" (胸肩). Some theories suggest that it originally referred to a water lagoon. Munakata Taisha was revered as the clan deity of the local people. It is said that when {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后|12=draft|12=draft}} prayed for safe passage during her {{ill|conquest of the Three Han|ja|三韓征伐|12=draft|12=draft}}, she experienced divine miracles, leading to the tradition of dispatching envoys to Munakata for rituals on significant occasions. Due to its importance, the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=draft|12=draft}} honored the shrine, and each time the imperial capital was relocated, its deity was enshrined in the {{ill|Kashiko-dokoro|ja|賢所|12=draft|12=draft}}, the imperial sanctuary. This highlights the deity’s reputation as a protector of maritime safety. With the introduction of the {{ill|Ritsuryō system|ja|律令制|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata was designated as a {{ill|shrine territory|ja|寺社領|12=draft|12=draft}}, and the {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|1=Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|12=draft|12=draft}}, a local ruling family, served as high priests while also governing the {{ill|shrine district|ja|神郡|12=draft|12=draft}}. According to an inscription on a stone monument recording the lineage of the Munakata clan, two generations of their chieftains married daughters of Chinese merchants. One of the clan members, {{ill|Munakata Tokuyoshi|ja|宗形徳善|12=draft|12=draft}}, offered his daughter, {{ill|Amako no Iratsume|ja|尼子娘|12=draft|12=draft}}, to Emperor {{ill|Tenmu|ja|Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu|12=draft|12=draft}} as a consort. Their first son, {{ill|Prince Takasaka|ja|高市皇子|12=draft|12=draft}}, born in {{ill|Hakuchi|ja|白雉|12=draft|12=draft}} 5 (654), played a crucial role in the {{ill|Jinshin War|ja|壬申の乱|12=draft|12=draft}}, earning high honors and later becoming the {{ill|Daijō-daijin|ja|太政大臣|12=draft|12=draft}}. {{ill|Prince Nagaya|ja|長屋王|12=draft|12=draft}} was his son, and he also became an ancestor of the {{ill|Takashina clan|ja|高階氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. By {{ill|Daido|ja|大同|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 (807), Munakata Taisha was granted 74 households in tribute. In {{ill|Jōwa|ja|承和|12=draft|12=draft}} 7 (840), it was promoted to {{ill|Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|ja|従五位下|1=Junior Fifth Rank|lt=Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade|12=draft|12=draft}}, and later, in {{ill|Jōgan|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} 1 (859), to {{ill|Senior Second Rank|ja|正二位|1=Senior Second Rank|12=draft|12=draft}}. Following the {{ill|Tengyō no Ran|ja|天慶の乱|12=draft|12=draft}} in {{ill|Tengyō|ja|天慶|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 (941), the shrine was further elevated to {{ill|Senior First Rank|ja|正一位|1=Senior First Rank|12=draft|12=draft}}, the highest divine rank. By {{ill|Tengen|ja|天元|12=draft|12=draft}} 2 (979), the position of {{ill|Ōmiya-shi|ja|大宮司|12=draft|12=draft}} (High Priest) was formally established by the {{ill|Dajōkan|ja|太政官|12=draft|12=draft}}. From the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|12=draft|12=draft}} onward, the Munakata clan, which had inherited the title of High Priest, became warriors and established themselves as powerful {{ill|kokujin lords|ja|国人領主|12=draft|12=draft}}. However, during the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, they were drawn into conflicts between the {{ill|Ōuchi clan|ja|大内氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, {{ill|Ōtomo clan|ja|大友氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, and {{ill|Shōni clan|ja|少弐氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, leading to Munakata Taisha becoming a target of military attacks. The shrine suffered multiple instances of arson and destruction, and the Munakata clan gradually declined. Nonetheless, with continued reverence from the {{ill|imperial court|ja|朝廷|12=draft|12=draft}} and the {{ill|samurai|ja|武家|12=draft|12=draft}}, it was repeatedly rebuilt. The present Hetsu Shrine {{ill|honden|ja|本殿|12=draft|12=draft}} with its beautiful {{ill|Kokerabuki|ja|こけら葺き|12=draft|12=draft}} thatched roof was reconstructed in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 6 (1578) by the High Priest {{ill|Munakata Ujisada|ja|宗像氏貞|12=draft|12=draft}}, while the {{ill|haiden|ja|拝殿|12=draft|12=draft}} was rebuilt in {{ill|Tenshō|ja|天正|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)|lt=Tenshō Era|12=draft|12=draft}} 16 (1590) by {{ill|Kobayakawa Takakage|ja|小早川隆景|12=draft|12=draft}}, the ruler of Chikuzen. Both structures are now designated {{ill|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ja|重要文化財|1=Important Cultural Property (Japan)|2=ja|3=重要文化財|lt=Important Cultural Property|qq= (Japan)|4=ko|5=일본의_중요문화재|12=draft|12=draft}}. After the decline of the Munakata clan, the {{ill|Kusakari clan|ja|草刈氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, including {{ill|Kusakari Shigetsugu|ja|草刈重継|12=draft|12=draft}}, succeeded their role in shrine rituals. During the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Kuroda clan|ja|黒田氏|12=draft|12=draft}}, lords of Chikuzen, repeatedly funded shrine reconstructions and land donations. Following the anti-Buddhist {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|12=draft|12=draft}} policies in the late {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata Taisha was separated from its associated {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|12=draft|12=draft}}, the {{ill|Chinkoku-ji|ja|鎮国寺|12=draft|12=draft}}. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 4 (1871), under the {{ill|modern shrine ranking system|ja|近代社格制度|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|12=draft|12=draft}}, Munakata Shrine was classified as a {{ill|National Middle Shrine|ja|国幣中社|12=draft|12=draft}}, before being promoted to {{ill|Imperial Middle Shrine|ja|官幣中社|12=draft|12=draft}} on April 22 the following year. In {{ill|Meiji|ja|明治|12=draft|12=draft}} 34 (1901), it was further elevated to {{ill|Imperial Grand Shrine|ja|官幣大社|12=draft|12=draft}}, the highest rank. After {{ill|World War II|ja|第二次世界大戦|12=draft|12=draft}}, the shrine grounds, which had fallen into disrepair, were restored thanks to donations from businessman {{ill|Idemitsu Sazō|ja|出光佐三|12=draft|12=draft}}, a native of Munakata. He also played a crucial role in advocating for national research and excavation of the Okinoshima ritual site. ==See also== *[[Itsukushima Shrine]] which was dedicated to the same goddesses *[[Munakata Saikaku]] *[[List of Shinto shrines]] *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (archaeological materials)]] *[[World Heritage Sites in Japan]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category-inline|Munakata-taisha}} {{Munakata Faith}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{draft categories| }} {{Kofun navbar}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Kofun template and pages that transclude it]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Fukuoka Prefecture]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese mythology]] [[Category:Expanded pages from Wikipedia]] [[Category:Pages goodbye $1 Wikipedia 2]] [[Category:qq]] [[Category:11]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Munakata, Fukuoka]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Taisha]] [[Category:Munakata Shrines]] [[Category:Nagare-zukuri]] [[Category:Munakata Taisha]] [[Category:Fixed Kofun templates]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:Pages goodbye $1 Wikipedia]] }} [[sn:Munakata Taisha]] [[ja:宗像大社]] [[en:Munakata Taisha]]
